outputs.L1:
I. *Ille Ego*

Oh, listen to me; for I am about  
To catch the fire of Chaucer,  
And spin out, in doleful measure,  
The tale of Johnny Raw, sir;  
Who, bent upon a desperate plan  
To make the people stare,  
Set off at full speed for Hindoostan  
Upon Old Poulter’s mare.

Tramp! tramp! across the land he went;  
Splash! splash! across the sea;  
And then he gave his boasting vent—  
“Pray, who can ride like me?

“For I am the man who sallied forth  
To rout the classic forces,  
And swore this mare was worth far more  
Than both fierce Hector’s horses.

“Old Homer from his throne I struck,  
To Virgil gave a punch,  
And in the place of both I set  
The doughty Mother Bunch.

“To France I galloped on my roan,  
Whose mettle nought could quail;  
There, squatting on the tomb of Joan,  
I piped a dismal tale.

“A wild and wondrous stave I sang,  
To make my hearers weep;  
But when I looked, and held my tongue,  
I found them fast asleep!

“Oh! then, a furious oath I swore,  
Some dire revenge to seek;  
And conjured up, to make them roar,  
Stout Taffy and his leek.

“To Heaven and Hell I rode away,  
In spite of wind and weather;  
Trumped up a diabolic lay,  
And cursed them all together.

“Now, Proteus! rise, thou changeful seer,  
To spirit up my mare:  
In every shape but those appear  
Which Taste and Nature wear.”
outputs.L2:
I. Ille Ego

Oh, hear me now, for I am set  
To kindle Chaucer’s flame,  
And in a mournful rhythm tell  
Young Johnny Raw’s strange fame;  
Who, fixed upon a reckless scheme  
To make the public gape,  
Rode off at racing speed toward Hindostan  
On ancient Poulter’s mare.

Thud, thud, he crossed the solid ground;  
Crash, splash, he crossed the foam;  
And then he burst into proud boasts:  
“Who rides as well as I?

“I am the fellow who set out  
To overthrow the ancient schools,  
And vowed this mare outvalued far  
The steeds of warlike Hector.

“I knocked old Homer from his seat,  
And dealt Virgil a blow;  
Then put in both their honored places  
The valiant Mother Bunch.

“To France I sped upon my roan,  
Whose spirit nothing daunts;  
There on the grave of Joan I crouched  
And played a gloomy strain.

“I sang a strange, astonishing song  
Designed to draw their tears;  
But when I paused and looked around,  
I saw them sound asleep.

“Then, in my rage, I swore a dreadful oath  
To hunt for some revenge;  
And raised, to make them laugh aloud,  
Brave Taffy with his leek.

“Through Heaven and through Hell I rode,  
Defying storm and wind;  
I patched together a devilish song  
And damned them all at once.

“Now, Proteus, shifting prophet, rise!  
Come rouse my mare with spirit;  
Take any form you choose to wear—  
Except the forms of Nature and of Taste.”
outputs.L3:
The poem presents itself as a comic literary undertaking, invoking Chaucer as a source of inspiration for a mock-heroic tale about Johnny Raw. By calling on such a revered figure at the beginning, the speaker gives the subject an exaggerated importance, as though Johnny’s adventures deserve to stand beside the great works of English literature. This immediately creates a humorous contrast between the grandeur of the poetic tradition and the absurdity of the hero being celebrated.

Johnny Raw’s journey is described in deliberately dramatic terms. He sets out for Hindoostan mounted not on a noble warhorse, but on Old Poulter’s mare, a detail that undercuts the heroic tone and turns the scene into comedy. His departure is not presented as a noble quest so much as a theatrical performance designed to impress the public. The poem mocks the desire for fame and attention by showing Johnny trying to appear grand and adventurous while the actual circumstances remain ridiculous.

The speaker’s own literary ambition is also treated satirically. He boasts that he can surpass the achievements of classical poets such as Homer and Virgil, suggesting that his poem will outdo the greatest epics of antiquity. This claim is clearly excessive, and the comedy lies in the mismatch between the speaker’s inflated confidence and the triviality of his subject. By imitating the language of epic poetry while applying it to an absurd tale, the poem exposes the vanity of writers who mistake loud ambition for genuine genius.

The speaker also attempts to create strong emotional effects through gloomy, wild, and dramatic songs. However, these efforts fail completely, since the audience responds not with awe or tears but by falling asleep. This comic failure shows that exaggerated emotional display does not necessarily produce real feeling. Instead of moving the audience, the speaker’s artificial intensity becomes tedious and ineffective.

Overall, the poem satirizes tasteless and exaggerated literary ambition. It contrasts empty spectacle with the qualities of true Taste and Nature, suggesting that genuine art depends on proportion, sincerity, and restraint rather than bombast. Through its mock-heroic treatment of Johnny Raw, its inflated comparisons to classical epic, and its comic scenes of failed emotional appeal, the poem ridicules writers who seek greatness through noise, display, and imitation rather than through authentic poetic skill.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a satire of “Johnny Raw,” a self-important would-be poet who mistakes noise, novelty, and exaggeration for true poetic genius. Johnny is eager to astonish his audience and to set himself apart from earlier writers, especially the classical models whose restraint, balance, and taste he rejects. Instead of learning from established forms or from nature, he tries to overwhelm readers with wild invention and theatrical display.

Much of the poem’s humor comes from its mock-heroic treatment of Johnny’s ambitions. He is described as if he were a great literary conqueror, riding through enormous and absurd poetic landscapes, confronting grand scenes, and performing with exaggerated confidence. Yet the heroic style only makes him appear more ridiculous, because his actual achievement is empty. The gap between the lofty language used to describe him and the poverty of his art exposes his vanity.

Johnny’s poetry depends on bombast: loud effects, strained images, and artificial excitement. He wants to shock and impress, but he lacks judgment, feeling, and genuine imaginative power. His rejection of classical examples is not a sign of originality but of ignorance. He confuses breaking rules with creating something new, and he assumes that extravagance alone can substitute for taste.

The audiences in the poem are not truly moved by his performances. They may be startled by his antics, but they are not persuaded, elevated, or emotionally affected. This failure is central to the satire. Poetry, the poem suggests, should be grounded in nature, human feeling, and artistic discipline. Without those qualities, even the most dramatic performance becomes hollow.

In the end, “Johnny Raw” becomes a comic example of false genius. His ambition is large, but his art is shallow. By mocking his inflated style and failed attempts at originality, the poem argues that novelty without judgment leads not to greatness but to ridicule. True poetry cannot be created through mere self-display; it requires taste, restraint, and a real connection to nature and human experience.
outputs.L5:
In Chaucer’s world, language is never merely a tool for telling stories; it is a way of shaping identity. The Latin words *ille* and *ego*—meaning “he” and “I”—can help us think about how Chaucer presents the self and the other in his poetry.

The word *ego* suggests the speaking “I”: the voice that claims authority, confesses weakness, or tells a tale. In *The Canterbury Tales*, Chaucer often plays with this idea. His narrator appears as an “I” who observes the pilgrims, describes their clothing and behavior, and records their stories. Yet this “I” is not always reliable. Chaucer’s narrator sometimes seems naïve, overly polite, or unwilling to judge openly. Through this uncertain *ego*, Chaucer creates humor and invites readers to think for themselves.

By contrast, *ille* points toward “he,” the figure being observed or described. Many of the pilgrims become an *ille*: the Knight, the Miller, the Pardoner, the Monk, and others. They are presented from the outside through details of speech, appearance, and action. But Chaucer’s genius lies in making these “he” figures complex. The Pardoner, for example, is not only a corrupt preacher; he is also a powerful speaker who understands his own hypocrisy. The Miller is crude and disruptive, yet his tale is full of energy and comic force.

The movement between *ego* and *ille* is central to Chaucer’s art. The narrator says “I,” but he spends much of his time describing “he” and “she.” In doing so, Chaucer explores the relationship between self and society. Each pilgrim tells a tale that reveals personal desires, social position, and moral outlook. The storyteller’s *ego* appears through the story told about others.

Although Chaucer wrote mainly in Middle English, not Latin, medieval readers lived in a multilingual culture where Latin still carried intellectual and religious authority. Words like *ego* and *ille* remind us of that background. They also highlight a timeless literary question: who is speaking, and who is being spoken about? In Chaucer, the answer is rarely simple. His poetry turns the gap between “I” and “he” into a space of irony, comedy, and deep human observation.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a mock-heroic satirical poem in archaic English, with Roman numeral section heading, about “Johnny Raw” riding Old Poulter’s mare to Hindoostan and boasting that he has surpassed Homer, Virgil, and Chaucer.
counterfactuals.output:
## I. THE HIGH ADVENTURE OF JOHNNY RAW

Sing, Muse, if Muse will stoop so low,  
Of Johnny Raw, that lordly crow,  
Who, mounted on Old Poulter’s mare,  
Did shake the dust and rend the air;  
And swore, by cap and rusty spur,  
No bard that ever breath’d could stir  
The world with such immortal strain  
As he should thunder o’er the plain.

Old Poulter’s mare, of ancient fame,  
A beast half wind, half joints, half shame,  
With one dim eye and tail awry,  
Did snort at Fate and blink at sky.  
Her ribs, like harp-strings, sadly rang,  
Her knees in antique couplets sprang;  
Yet Johnny cried, “Behold! I ride  
Where Cæsar’s self had turn’d aside!”

To Hindoostan his course he bent,  
With mighty heart and little sense;  
His saddle-bags were stuff’d with bread,  
A cracked gazette, and dreams ill-bred.  
He took the moon for eastern fire,  
The village pond for Ganges’ mire,  
And, seeing geese beside the way,  
Cried, “Lo! the elephants at play!”

“Make room,” quoth he, “ye sons of song!  
Your wreaths have crown’d the weak too long.  
Old Homer nods, and Virgil pales,  
And Chaucer tells but ale-house tales.  
I, Johnny Raw, with quill and rein,  
Have split the empyrean in twain;  
My verse shall make the planets jar,  
And shame the morning’s brightest star!”

Then up he rose in stirrups thin,  
A conqueror of his own blown din,  
And lash’d the mare, whose noble speed  
Scarce overtook a browsing weed.  
The sparrows laugh’d from hedge and thorn,  
The oxen look’d exceeding worn;  
The very sign-post creak’d, “Good sir,  
Thy glory hath a foolish spur.”

Yet on he clatter’d, proud and stark,  
Through turnpike mud and twilight dark,  
Proclaiming still, with brazen cheer,  
“No bard before me hath come near!  
Let Homer keep his Grecian ghost,  
Let Mantua’s swan resign his boast,  
Let Chaucer quit his pilgrim throng—  
Raw is the emperor of song!”

At last, when night her curtain drew,  
And all his eastern empire flew,  
He found, not Ind, nor jewell’d throne,  
But Poulter’s yard, with hens full-grown.  
The mare, right glad the war was done,  
Stood munching straw beneath the sun;  
While Johnny, fallen in the mire,  
Still crown’d himself Apollo’s sire.

So ends the march, the bardic roar,  
The steed, the boast, the boundless lore:  
Let future ages mark with awe  
The deathless name of Johnny Raw—  
Who rode a mare of Poulter’s stall  
To Hindoostan, yet stirr’d not at all;  
And, ere he’d pass’d the parish border,  
Put Homer, Virgil, Chaucer, in order.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an 18th-century-style burlesque ballad beginning “Ille Ego Oh!” that parodies a pompous poet’s journey across land and sea, including references to Hector’s horses, Mother Bunch, Joan of Arc, Taffy and his leek, Heaven, Hell, and Proteus.
counterfactuals.output:
Ille Ego Oh! — with a hey nonny nose,  
A Poet set forth in his ruffles and prose;  
His wig was a tempest, his cane was a spear,  
And he vow’d to out-thunder the spheres in one year.  

He mounted, for want of Apollo’s bright team,  
Two nags that had Hector’s old horses in dream;  
“Xanthus! Podargus!” he cried in a heat,  
While they stumbled on turnpikes and browsed at his feet.  

To Mother Bunch’ cupboard he next made a call,  
Where legends hung pickle’d in smoke on the wall;  
She gave him a crust and a thimble of ale,  
And sold him a prophecy, three-pence the tale.  

“Go conquer,” quoth she, “both the land and the flood;  
Write oceans in ink, and write kingdoms in mud;  
Let Critics, those Cerberus-whelps, snarl and rail—  
A Bard with a bladder may weather a gale.”  

Then over the downs like a comet he past,  
Till his sublime hat was blown off by the blast;  
He follow’d it weeping through furrow and brake,  
As Taffy once follow’d his national leek.  

There Taffy himself, with his leek in his hat,  
Cried, “Cot pless your Muse, sir, but what would you be at?  
If glory be dinner, then glory is thin;  
Put leek in your ballad, and supper comes in.”  

He cross’d to the shore in a chaise without springs,  
Declaring the pebbles inferior things;  
Then hired a cockle-shell, leaky and wide,  
And christen’d it “Pindar,” and puff’d on the tide.  

The Sea, like a printer, struck off in a sheet,  
Dash’d commas of brine at his elegant feet;  
The winds turn’d reviewers, and whistled so keen,  
They tore his last ode into cantos thirteen.  

He call’d upon Proteus, that slippery blade,  
Who into a porpoise, a parson, a maid,  
A critic, a lobster, a duchess, a kite,  
Transform’d, and still answer’d, “Your verses are trite.”  

Then Joan of Arc, arm’d with a pudding-spoon lance,  
Rose up from a billow and taught him to dance;  
“March on,” cried the Maid, “with thy trumpet of tin—  
A hero is known by the noise he is in.”  

He storm’d then at Heaven, and knock’d at the gate:  
“Pray enter,” said Peter, “but first leave your weight—  
Your similes, epics, and prefaces tall;  
For baggage so mighty would founder us all.”  

He flounc’d down to Hell in poetical ire,  
And ask’d a snug corner to kindle his fire;  
But Pluto laugh’d out, with a brimstone-lac’d bow,  
“We burn not such paper; ’tis smoky enow.”  

Back, back o’er the billows, by moonshine and foam,  
Our Bard and his bladder came bobbing toward home;  
He landed, proclaiming, with solemn grimace,  
That Europe had trembled at sight of his face.  

Now Hector’s dull horses are grazing in peace,  
And Taffy has supp’d on his leek and his cheese;  
Dame Bunch shuts her book, Joan returns to her rest,  
And Proteus turns critic—which shape suits him best.  

Ille Ego Oh! let the punch-bowl go round,  
For pride is a drum with a very small sound;  
Who rides over earth, and sails over sea,  
May end where he started—at vanity’s knee.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a rhymed comic poem in the style of a literary satire, where a foolish bard on a mare attacks the classics, puts audiences to sleep, and ends by invoking Proteus while rejecting Taste and Nature.
counterfactuals.output:
A bard there was, of addled air,  
Who rode a philosophic mare;  
With ink-stained spur and paper shield,  
He challenged Homer in the field.  

“Come down, old Greeks!” the blockhead cried,  
While sideways on his nag he plied;  
“I’ll mend your measures, purge your fire,  
And tune the tragic to my lyre!”  

The mare, more wise than he by half,  
Replied with one judicious laugh;  
Yet on he bounced through dust and din,  
To rout dead poets with his chin.  

He called the epics “lengthy stuff,”  
Found Virgil smooth, but not enough;  
Declared that Sophocles lacked art,  
And Shakespeare “missed the modern heart.”  

Then to the town he made his way,  
To give a reading—twice a day;  
The benches groaned, the candles wept,  
The very fiddler bowed and slept.  

He sang of clouds that would not rain,  
Of kings who lost a borrowed chain,  
Of shepherds pale, and nymphs in boots,  
And metaphors with tangled roots.  

One critic snored behind his hat;  
A duchess dreamed she was a cat;  
The mayor, to prove his civic zeal,  
Applauded softly with his heel.  

Still louder rose the bard’s refrain:  
“Your Taste is but a courtly chain!  
Your Nature—pah!—a village rule  
Invented to oppress the fool.  

“Let pedants praise the balanced line,  
The living stream, the old design;  
I scorn their gardens, trimmed and straight—  
Give me the swamp, and call it Fate!”  

His mare then sneezed; the rafters shook,  
A sleeping usher dropped his book;  
The lamps burned low, the watchman swore,  
And Silence locked the outer door.  

At last, in triumph, pale and hoarse,  
He slid, like gravy, from his horse,  
And cried, “O Proteus! shift my name,  
My shape, my sense—but keep my fame!  

“Let Taste be drowned, let Nature flee;  
Change all the world—excepting me!”  
Then, crowned with hay and loud applause,  
He bowed to no one’s waking jaws.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you imitate an old-fashioned mock epic verse form and produce Section I of a poem about Johnny Raw, a bragging rider who travels to Hindoostan, France, Heaven, and Hell on Old Poulter’s mare?
counterfactuals.output:
## JOHNNY RAW; OR, OLD POULTER’S MARE  
### Section I

I sing—what Muse shall deign to loose my jaw?—  
The thund’ring feats of gallant Johnny Raw;  
A blade so bold, that, when his tongue was free,  
He made the moon look pale with modesty.  
No tavern-bench but shook beneath his boast,  
No chimney-corner but had heard his ghost  
Of deeds half-done, and dangers never near,  
And armies routed by a wink and leer.

He swore he’d crossed the seas without a sail,  
Had boxed a shark, and twisted off its tail;  
Had dined with kings, had bullied dukes and earls,  
And taught the Pope to whistle jigs for girls;  
Had drunk the Danube dry in half a night,  
And beat a thunderbolt in open fight.  
Thus Johnny talk’d; while all who heard him there  
Cried, “Mount, brave Raw!—mount Old Poulter’s mare!”

Now Old John Poulter kept, behind the mill,  
A beast of fame, though somewhat past her will:  
One eye had she, and that was dim and red,  
A broom-like tail, a melancholy head;  
Her ribs, like hoops on some old cider-cask,  
Were plain enough for any child to ask;  
Yet in her heart there lurk’d, so gossips say,  
A fire that Time had never whipp’d away.

“Bring forth,” quoth Raw, “the courser of renown!  
I’ll ride her straight to Hindoostan town;  
From thence to France, where fiddlers scrape and bow,  
Then up to Heaven, and—if I’m spared—below.  
Let cowards keep the road and count the stones;  
I’ll make a turnpike of the dead men’s bones.  
The sun shall mend my spur, the stars shall stare,  
When Johnny Raw bestrides old Poulter’s mare!”

He spoke: the stable-door flew wide with dread,  
The hens all cackled, and the house-dog fled;  
The mare came forth, and with a solemn cough  
Blew three old cobwebs from her nostrils off.  
Raw leapt aloft—so prodigies begin—  
His hat cock’d out, his elbows sharp as sin;  
Then smack’d his whip, and cried, with lordly air,  
“Make way for Raw, and Old John Poulter’s mare!”
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a Georgian-era parody poem with quatrains and comic exclamations like “Tramp! tramp!” and “Splash! splash!”, lampooning a bad poet who claims to dethrone Homer and Virgil and replace them with Mother Bunch.
counterfactuals.output:
Behold the Bard, with wig awry,  
Who storms Parnassus after lunch;  
“Down, Homer! Virgil, pack and fly!  
Make room,” cries he, “for Mother Bunch!”  

**Tramp! tramp!** he mounts the Muses’ stair,  
With ink-pot, goose-quill, hat, and crutch;  
The Nine peep out and cry, “Take care!  
His verses limp exceeding much!”  

He vows the Iliad’s but a toy,  
The Æneid fit for pastry-punch;  
“True epic fire,” declares the boy,  
“Burns brightest in Dame Mother Bunch!”  

**Splash! splash!** his couplets fall in pools,  
And drown the sense in muddy sound;  
Apollo sends him back to schools,  
But still he bawls and struts around.  

“Great Homer nods!”—“Then I shall reign!”  
He thumps his breast with awful hunch;  
“Let Mantua’s swan forsake the plain,  
And cackle now with Mother Bunch!”  

**Clang! clang!** his rhymes, like pots at fair,  
Beat time to nonsense, bold and broad;  
The critics gape, the ladies stare,  
And footmen laugh behind the board.  

He crowns himself with laurel-leek,  
Recites till candles gutter down;  
His Muse, with snuff upon her cheek,  
Mistakes a nightcap for a crown.  

**Bang! bang!** he strikes the epic lyre,  
It answers with a kitchen-crunch;  
“Immortal fame is my desire—  
And marmalade with Mother Bunch!”  

So let him reign in Grub Street’s hall,  
Where dunces dine and debtors munch;  
While Homer, Virgil, gods and all,  
Sneak off to tea with Mother Bunch.
